newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's Socialists scramble for Gonzalez successor.
newsitem.headline: Spain's Socialists scramble for Gonzalez successor.

text.p: Spain's Socialists met into the early hours of Saturday, scrambling to find a new leader for their party after Felipe Gonzalez announced he would not run again for party chief.

The party has less than 48 hours to come up with a replacement for the former prime minister who shocked party members on Friday by announcing he would not run for re-election after heading the party for 24 years and leading Spain for 13 of those.

"We have to be able in these two days to see which person will take the position of secretary-general. It's not going to be easy, because of Felipe's level of leadership and calibre in all aspects," former Socialist social affairs minister Cristina Alberdi told Reuters.
At the party's 34th Congress which opened on Friday, Gonzalez told delegates it was time for "a change of generations" in the Socialist leadership. "Please replace me," he urged.

But the 55 year-old Gonzalez gave no hint as to a possible successor and his move unleashed a leadership battle that will decide who will take the Socialists into the next general election scheduled for the year 2000.
The Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) executive committee met late on Friday to start compiling a list of possible candidates for the leadership and to shape the next executive committee.
A final list of candidates is expected to emerge late on Saturday or early Sunday and Socialist delegates must vote in their new leadership on Sunday -- the final day of the congress.
Still Spain's most popular politician, Gonzalez was widely expected to be re-elected at the three-day congress.

But although his decision stunned many party members, delegates agreed it was a necessary step to breathe new life into the demoralised Socialist movement which lost to Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar's conservative Popular Party in a general election last year.
"He made a great gesture for democracy and for Spain," Socialist parliamentary president Joaquin Almunia said.
No clear front-runners have since emerged, but delegates toyed with a number of names.
"It could be Almunia, it could be another colleague, but I think there are many good candidates and many people who could take over under these circumstances," Alberdi said.
Almunia was one name frequently mentioned by delegates. But Almunia would not say if he would run as a candidate.
"Talk of me running as secretary general has no foundation and no credibility as it is very early on in the congress," Almunia told reporters.
Two obvious candidates were regional leaders Jose Bono of Castille La Mancha and Manuel Chaves of Andalusia, but some delegates pointed out that both lacked nationwide recognition.

The party's high profile former government spokesman Alfredo Perez Rubalcaba was another candidate, although delegates said he had been tainted by a succession of corruption scandals which contributed to the downfall of the last Socialist administration.
Organisational secretary Cipria Ciscar could present the party with a fresh face, having never served in government, delegates said.

Delegates also mentioned NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister, as one of the best qualified candidates, but said they thought it unlikely he would give up his role as NATO Secretary General.
